title: Adapter sidecar ownership playbook
body:
Purpose:
This note explores a pragmatic ownership model for runtime adapters implemented as sidecars, clarifies control-plane vs data-plane boundaries, and lists handoffs required for multi-region routing and failover. Intended audience: platform eng, serving runtime, api-gateway, and SREs.

Context and motivation:
- We are seeing repeated ownership confusion on incidents involving adapter upgrades, routing rules, and per-region fallbacks.
- Pattern proposed: lightweight sidecar adapter processes (per-node or per-runtime pool) that encapsulate model-specific wiring and expose a consistent runtime adapter API to the control plane.
- Goal: reduce cross-team coupling, make clear SLO ownership, and simplify multi-region routing decisions.

High-level service boundary proposal (informal):
- API Gateway: owner = api-gateway team. Responsibilities: external auth/ingress, rate limiting, top-level routing decision to a control-plane endpoint. Not responsible for per-model readiness beyond simple upstream health checks.
- Control Plane / Orchestrator: owner = platform-orchestration subteam. Responsibilities: policy evaluation (cost/latency/region), model versioning, rollout control, global routing policy (which region/cluster to use), and issuing route tokens to runtime. Not responsible for kernel-level inference logic.
- Runtime Adapters (sidecars): owner = serving-runtime team (runtime-adapters subteam). Responsibilities: implement the adapter API (load model variant, manage KV cache lifecycle, local batching coordinator, hardware affinity hints), health checks (detailed readiness), per-adapter metrics exposed to control plane, and graceful drain hooks.

Key adapter API contract (sketch):
- /healthz: simple up/down for gateway; returns 200 when adapter process alive (gateway uses this).
- /ready: richer readiness (model loaded, enough memory, batch queue ok). Control plane relies on this for routing decisions.
- /route-decision: control-plane -> sidecar: attach runtime hints (max-batch, quant profile, fallback-model-list). Sidecar returns accept/reject and estimated latency.
- /metrics: Prometheus-style endpoint including per-model tokens/sec, avg-latency-ms, queue-depth, kv-cache-hits.

Routing decision flow (normal):
1) Gateway -> Control Plane: incoming request metadata (customer tier, region preference, SLO requirements).
2) Control Plane evaluates policies (latency SLO, cost target, data residency), selects candidate region/pool, queries sidecar /route-decision for a small set (2-3) of runtime nodes to get fast estimates.
3) Control Plane chooses a node, returns route token to Gateway which forwards request directly to runtime (data-plane path) using short-lived token.

Fallback / degradation modes:
- If sidecar /ready returns false for model X in region A, control plane should attempt region B if allowed by policy.
- If all regions show degraded readiness, automatic fallback to a smaller model variant or lower-quality quantized profile (as allowed by customer policy).
- If route-token verification fails at runtime, gateway should fallback to another route or return a graceful degradation payload (early-exit message).

Multi-region considerations and ownership implications:
- Data residency constraints must be encoded in policy store (ownership: security-and-compliance + platform-orchestration). Platform eng owns enforcement at decision-time; compliance owns the rules.
- Regional capacity signals: sidecars own local capacity estimation; they publish summarized capacity metrics to control plane collector every 30s. Control plane owns global capacity view and routing prioritization.
- Failover SLAs: SRE owns cross-region failover playbooks and runbooks; platform-orchestration owns automated fallback wiring.

Operational handoffs and runbook snippets (who does what):
- Upgrading adapter sidecar image: serving-runtime owns release artifact. Platform-eng schedules canary rollouts via orchestration with canary percentage and health gating. SRE owns incident playbook and rollback triggers.
- Model hot-swap (in-region): runtime-adapters own model load/unload behavior; orchestration owns version pinning and rollout policy.
- Policy change (routing weight change): platform-orchestration owns change; api-gateway executes modified routing tables. Add a pre-change checklist (impact analysis, smoke tests, rollback plan).

SLO/metric mapping to owners (proposal):
- Per-request P95 latency (gateway->runtime end-to-end): owners = api-gateway (ingress latency), serving-runtime (inference latency), platform-orchestration (routing-induced latency).
- Model load time: owner = runtime-adapters.
- Route token acceptance ratio: owner = platform-orchestration (issuance logic) + runtime-adapters (validation).
- Capacity headroom: owner = runtime-adapters (local measurement) + platform-orchestration (aggregation + autoscale trigger).

Testing and validation matrix (minimal):
- Unit tests for adapter API contract (mocked control plane).
- Integration: control-plane staging -> sidecar staging with synthetic load tests that emulate multi-region latency.
- Chaos: inject slow /ready responses, simulate KV cache thrashing, and validate control plane fallback logic.

Migration plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (quick wins): define and publish adapter API spec, add basic /ready and /metrics endpoints to current adapters.
- Phase 1 (canary): add route-decision endpoint, deploy to a single pool; have control plane call into sidecars for soft routing hints only (no strict dependency).
- Phase 2 (enforcement): control plane begins to rely on /ready for routing; gateway disallows traffic to nodes where /ready=false.
- Phase 3 (multi-region rollout): enable cross-region decisioning with residency blocklists, run a week of shadow traffic before full cutover.

Open questions / TODOs (short):
- Do we standardize a protobuf contract or keep JSON over HTTP? (TODO: short spike, 1 week)
- Security: signing of route tokens and replay resistance. Who stores keys? (TODO: KMS integration design with security team)
- Observability: how to correlate request traces across gateway->control-plane->runtime without adding large overhead? (TODO: sampling strategy)
- Ownership edge cases: who owns drain-related customer-facing error messages? (document required)

Appendix: quick incident example (notes)
- Symptom: model requests from region eu-west experienced 20% 5xxs after a serving-runtime deploy.
- Initial triage: gateway saw token acceptance failures; control plane logs showed sidecars returning late readiness for new quant profile.
- Fix: rollback adapter image, restart pool, and schedule a constrained canary.
- Postmortem action items: add early preflight for quant profile in staging; add readiness warmup timer in sidecars.

Last notes and next steps:
- Requesting review from serving-runtime and api-gateway leads.
- Proposed meeting: Platform-Ownership sync (Nov 12) to align on API schema and canary strategy.
- If we land on a protobuf + gRPC approach, add a compatibility policy for gradual transitions.

References and links:
- Confluence: Control Plane Service Map (see linked_artifacts)
- PR: platform/pull/842 (adapter health endpoint changes)
- Jira: JIRA-PLAT-231 (routing policy enforcement epic)

(Working draft; intentionally informal and pragmatic — comments welcome.)
